job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Freya Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Freya, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a terraced house in Calder, shared with two other women, and I've turned the corner of it into a candle workshop. Mornings I pour candles and photograph them, and an AI tool helps me write the shop listings and answer customer messages. Afternoons I apply for jobs and do social posts for two stallholders at the Saturday market. Evenings I go to the youth group at our church, and I'm often the one who runs the bake sale.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up making candles, and what was your degree?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a bachelor's in business with a marketing focus at Calder University and passed with an average mark, no internship, since I worked at the market all through my studies. My grandfather had a hardware shop, and I grew up thinking you make your own luck by selling something. The candles bring in about a hundred and fifty pounds a month after costs, and the posting work adds sixty. My loan is huge, my savings would last about a week, and my family has nothing to spare, so I'm the one who sends a bit home when I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and a lot of noise, which is how most new things go. I'd tell the girls at church that you still need to work hard, and no machine will do that for you. Online I'd keep posting my candles and say how I use it, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means I'm slightly ahead of other applicants because I use the tools every day, but the shortage of jobs is the same. There are very few marketing posts in Calder, and the ones that exist want experience. So I'd carry on building my own thing, since waiting for someone to hire me isn't working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the candle business harder, aiming for three hundred pounds a month by spring, with a stall at the Saturday market and a better online shop. I'd keep the two stallholders as clients and try to add a third, perhaps the florist on Mill Street. I'd apply for five jobs a week, in case something real comes along. And I'd keep helping at church, because the community has always helped me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driven, a bit tired. I like building, and I hate sitting waiting. The loan sits in the corner of my mind, like a bill taped to the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What do you make of the idea that it's hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the money in the thin months. Candles sell well before Christmas and badly in January. If I had a proper salary, I'd have a cushion, and I'd have more courage to put money into the business. Right now every pound I spend on wax is a pound that doesn't go to the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the part of your plan you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the market manager for a bigger stall and a better spot near the entrance. I'd also make a simple price list and a small set of gift boxes, because they sell for more. And I'd ask the church to put my cards on their notice board, which they'd do happily.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but noisy**, and no machine will do the hard work for you.
I'd keep posting candles and say how I use it.
think: I'm slightly ahead because I use the tools daily, but **job shortage** is the same.
Waiting for someone to hire me isn't working, so I build my own thing.
do: Push the candle business to **three hundred pounds** a month by spring.
Ask the market manager for a bigger stall and add a third client, the florist on Mill Street.
Apply for five jobs a week in case something real comes.
feel: **Driven**, a bit tired: I hate sitting and waiting, and the loan sits like a bill on the fridge.

fieldNote: She is an **entrepreneur** at heart and trusts work over handouts.

steps.text: Get a bigger stall at the Saturday market

Apply for five marketing jobs a week
Keep running the church bake sale and community stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we should use it, not fear it. I'd tell people at church that they shouldn't wait for someone to rescue them, but they should help one another learn. I'd post my own tips online, because I think people respect someone who shows how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm excited and uneasy. The tasks in an entry marketing job, like writing copy, scheduling and customer replies, are the ones I already do with AI in minutes. That's good for my own business, but a firm would need one person where it used to need three. I'd compete with those firms for clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further with my own tools: automated customer replies, product photos and listings made faster so I can make more candles. I'd offer a small package to market stallholders, helping them with posts and a simple online shop for a monthly fee. And I'd study a short course in e-commerce and data, because the next step is knowing which products sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite energised, honestly. I like it when things move, because people like me with nothing to lose can get ahead of the ones who are comfortable. But I'd feel for friends who aren't comfortable with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How exposed is your own business to this change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own business is exposed in a good way, as the tools make me faster. But my customers are also exposed, because people buy fewer luxuries when they're nervous about jobs. If the market stallholders lose trade, I lose clients. I'd be in the same weather as them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from government, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want light rules: don't let big firms bury small ones, and help with training that actually leads to work. I'm not for handouts, I'd rather have an apprenticeship scheme or small-business loans. People should be paid for work, not for waiting.

say: I'd say it's real, so **use it**, not fear it, and help one another learn.
I'd post my tips online, since people respect someone who shows how.
think: The tasks in an entry marketing job are ones I already do with AI in **minutes**.
A firm would need one person where it needed three, so I'd compete with those firms for clients.
do: Automate customer replies and speed up **product photos** and listings.
Offer stallholders a monthly package for posts and a simple online shop.
Study a short course in e-commerce and data.
feel: **Energised**, though I'd feel for friends who aren't comfortable with the tools.
S1.quote: People should be paid for work, not for waiting.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **force multiplier** for her own stall and clients.
Wants light rules and apprenticeships, not handouts.

steps.text: Automate candle shop customer replies and listings
Sell stallholders a monthly social posts and online shop package
Take a short e-commerce and data course
Write to my MP asking for small-business loans for young people

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, church, neighbours and family, and tell the government to move fast with support. I'd say people should not wait. I'd also say employers have to be honest and keep paying people who still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be alarmed, even though I'm used to the tools. If almost all thinking work is done by AI in two years, there's no marketing job to apply for, and the customers who buy candles might have no income. My cushion is a week. I'd have to make something that people still want when money is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd take any paid work going, weekend market shifts, cleaning or catering at church events. I'd put all my candle profits into savings. I'd also look for hands-on products, like candles and baking, that people want when times are hard, because machines take three more years to do those. And I'd call the loan company about a payment holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit raw. I'd tell myself I've been through worse, but at night I'd run the numbers. I'd also pray, and ask for strength to look after my parents, who I help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older people at church who live on pensions, and the stallholders who live day to day. Families where both parents work in offices would be hit first. I'd organise meals and a swap table, and I'd be the person who knows how to run the posts and the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your community would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfort things sell, like candles, bread and small gifts. I'd rather sell something handmade than be a junior in an office that won't exist. So I'd double down on the business and see if I can make it carry me, even at a basic level.

say: I'd say we need to **look after each other** and tell the government to move fast on support.
Employers must keep paying people who still work.
think: With thinking work done by AI, there's **no marketing job** to apply for, and buyers may have no income.
My cushion is a week, so I'd need something people want when money is tight.
do: Take any paid work: market shifts, cleaning or **church catering**.
Put all candle profits into savings and call the loan company about a payment holiday.
Focus on hands-on products people want in hard times.
feel: **Anxious and raw**, running the numbers at night and praying for strength.
S2.quote: I'd rather sell something handmade than be a junior in an office that won't exist.
fieldNote: Her answer turns to **community care**: meals, a swap table, church events.
Doubles down on handmade goods, which robots reach later.
The week-long cushion keeps her mood **high**, even with strong skills.

steps.text: Take weekend market and church catering shifts for steady pay
Put every candle profit into savings
Call the loan company about a payment holiday
Organise meals and a swap table through the church

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and we should use it. I'd tell people to learn a skill that involves people, and I'd tell firms to take on trainees. I'd say it at church and to anyone who listens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm cautiously hopeful. In five years I could build a real small business, with a few staff and a market stall in two towns. I wouldn't be depending on a firm that might close its junior roles. I'd be a seller with a name people know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the business in steps: an online shop that runs mostly itself, a stall at two markets, and a small team of one or two part-timers. I'd save a hundred and fifty pounds a month, pay down the loan, and keep looking for a part-time marketing job for stable income. I'd also learn bookkeeping properly, since I'll need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up, with a bit of fear. I can plan something real, which is a good feeling. It's the first scenario where I feel I'm the one steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for your candle business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More time means I can try, fail and try again. In two years I'd have to be careful with every pound. With five I could invest in a small kiln of candles, a better camera and a proper website. I'd also try new products, like wax melts and gift boxes, and see what sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still look for a job, or go all in on the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, for the first year or two. A part-time job gives me a steady income and a reference, and the business grows on the side. Then, when it can pay me a living, I'd move to it full time. I'd rather have a net under me.

say: I'd say five years is **fair warning**, so use it, and learn a skill involving people.
I'd tell firms to take on trainees.
think: I could build a real small business with a few staff and a market stall in **two towns**.
I wouldn't depend on a firm that might close its junior roles.
do: Grow in steps: an online shop that runs mostly itself and **stalls in two markets**.
Save £150 a month and pay down the loan.
Keep a part-time marketing job for steady income and learn bookkeeping.
feel: **Fired up**, with a bit of fear, and steering for once.
S3.quote: In five years I could build a real small business, with a few staff and a market stall in two towns.
fieldNote: Longer warning lets her **invest** in the business step by step.

steps.text: Open stalls at two markets and an automated online shop
Save £150 a month and pay down the loan
Hire one part-timer once the business covers wages
Take a part-time marketing job for steady income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so work hard, learn the tools, and don't let anyone tell you you're too young. I'd say we should teach each other, young and old. I'd say it with a smile, because I'd honestly feel good about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I'm in a strong position. By thirty-three I could own a small business with a real name, maybe a shop in Calder and an online store, and I'd employ three people. I'd also be married, with the first child on the way. It takes a lot, but I think it's reachable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the business and a part-time job, save two hundred pounds a month and pay the loan down in about four years. I'd learn accounting, so I can keep the books myself, and use AI for the daily work. I'd also keep up my church work, and help neighbours start small ventures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, in a steady way. The loan still sits there, but I'd feel I can beat it. It's the one picture where I feel I have time for a family too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what does your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small shop on Mill Street with my name on the sign, a husband who also works hard, and a child sleeping in a basket behind the till, like my grandfather's days. Maybe a small team. And I'd still go to the market on Saturdays to say hello.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the girls in your youth group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start something small now, whether it's baking, sewing or a service, and to learn the tools. I'd say don't wait for permission, and be honest with customers. And I'd tell them that faith helps, but it isn't a substitute for work.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so **work hard**, learn the tools and don't wait.
I'd say young and old should teach each other.
think: By thirty-three I could own a small business with a **real name**, a shop in Calder and an online store.
I could also be married with a first child on the way.
do: Start with the business and a part-time job, saving two hundred pounds a month.
Pay the loan down in about **four years** and learn accounting to keep the books myself.
Help neighbours start small ventures through church.
feel: **Hopeful**, in a steady way: I can beat the loan and have time for a family.
S4.quote: I'd tell them to start something small now, whether it's baking, sewing or a service, and to learn the tools.
fieldNote: The decade lets her picture **business and family** together, which no other scenario allows.
Her style is practical and faith-led, with work first.

steps.text: Open a small shop on Mill Street with my name on the sign
Save two hundred pounds a month and clear the loan in four years
Learn accounting and use AI for daily tasks
Plan to marry and start a family once the shop is steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I'd have a week of savings and the people who buy my candles would be anxious. What would help is a payment holiday on the loan, small-business loans for young people and a community that holds together. Honest information about what's coming would help most.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not asking anyone to carry me. I use the tools, I work every day, and I still have no safety net. A small business loan with fair terms would do more for people like me than any speech.

headlineQuote: I'm not asking anyone to carry me. I use the tools, I work every day, and I still have no safety net.
portrait: Freya (23) rents a shared room in **Calder** and runs a candle workshop in the corner of it.
She holds a pass in business and marketing, owes a huge loan and has about a week of savings.
She uses **AI every day**, earns about two hundred pounds a month from candles and posts, and works hard.
She is traditional and **faith-led**, trusts work over handouts and wants fair small-business loans.
She plans an entrepreneurial path in every scenario, and her mood eases only when ten years give her room.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most because she has a week of savings and her customers would be anxious.
whatWouldHelp: A loan **payment holiday**, small-business loans for young people and honest information.
